events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Sam. As leader I'm taking a seat on the first mission to share the risk, and I'm pairing myself with Sam, who has been steady so far. Two members keeps the team small for an early mission, and I'll explain the choice in discussion.

I appreciate Leo taking a seat to share the risk — that's a solid leadership move. But I want to flag some hesitation about pairing Leo with Sam specifically. On Mission 1 we have very little public information to go on, and putting the two most committed voices together means if either is compromised, we have no cross-check within the team. I'd prefer a team that mixes someone taking responsibility (like Leo) with someone we can later compare against — someone whose play we can track across missions. Sam, what's your reasoning for being comfortable on this opening team, and why should the group trust that pairing over alternatives?

Omar, fair question. I'm comfortable because Mission 1 is exactly when a small team can be most transparent: Leo is taking public responsibility as leader, and I'm on the record as the second member. That gives the table two named players to evaluate from the first proposal rather than anonymous risk. I understand the cross-check concern, but with only two seats there is no third member inside the team to cross-check either way; the cross-check comes from the public votes and the mission result. If this team is approved, I will judge it by the mission outcome, not by pre-emptive suspicion. I don't think there is enough public evidence to reject the leader's opening pair; a rejection now mainly burns time and moves leadership without a clearer alternative. If anyone has concrete evidence against Leo or me, they should state it; otherwise I'm inclined to support the proposal and let Mission 1 produce information.

I'm not comfortable with this team. Omar raised a solid point and Sam's response actually reinforces it — Sam dismissed the concern about cross-checking but didn't address why the two of them together is better than splitting them up. Leo and Sam, you're both asking the table to simply trust you, but we have zero information to go on right now, and that's exactly the moment where we should be most cautious about concentration of power. If Leo is Evil, he'd want Sam on the team too. If Sam is Evil, he'd want to be on Leo's team. The whole point of the leader sharing risk is to spread it around — but here both seats are held by players who have been the most vocal and aligned. I'd prefer Amara or Kenji mixed in with one of them so we get fresh perspectives and aren't putting all our early eggs in one basket. Nothing personal against either of you, but the concentration should worry everyone at this table.

I want to be very direct: I am voting against Leo, Sam. Look at what has happened in this discussion. Leo proposes himself and Sam. Sam immediately defends the team. Leo and Sam are aligned on this. That is the pattern I warned about. When two players back each other without hesitation on the very first mission, we should ask why. Leo, you say you're sharing risk — but putting yourself with Sam doesn't share risk, it concentrates it. Sam, you said rejection 'burns time' — that's pressure to rubber-stamp. On Mission 1, a rejection costs us nothing but a new leader. This is exactly the moment to be cautious, not compliant. I'm asking the rest of the table — Amara, Kenji — take a serious look at this pair. If either is compromised, this team fails immediately with no room for correction. I'd rather see Leo paired with someone he hasn't already aligned with, or Sam swapped out entirely. The fact that neither of them has offered an alternative or shown any willingness to reconsider tells me they want this exact team through. That should concern everyone.

Omar has now repeated the same objection three times: that Leo and I are aligned, therefore the team should be rejected. That is not concrete evidence; it is a narrative built from the fact that I answered his question directly. On Mission 1, every approval decision is made with almost no public information, so rejecting a team mainly moves leadership and spends discussion without producing a mission result. Omar says rejection costs nothing, but it costs the table the only real information we can get now: whether this team succeeds or fails. I support Leo, Sam because the leader is taking public responsibility and the team is small enough to evaluate immediately. If Omar has specific evidence against Leo or me, he should state it plainly rather than treating alignment and confidence as proof of wrongdoing. His repeated push to reject before any mission result is more suspicious to me than the opening pair itself.

Omar, I hear the concern about concentration, but a two-person team is the least risky way to start Mission 1. Only two cards are played, so there's no hidden third seat to hide behind. I took the seat myself, so I'm not asking anyone to carry a risk I won't carry. Swapping in a stranger now wouldn't give us better information. It would just reshuffle the same unknowns and burn a rejection. I also don't think the pattern of Sam and me backing each other is evidence on its own. We're both answering the same objection directly. The honest test is the mission result, and we'll all learn from it whichever way it goes. Kenji, you haven't weighed in yet. Do you see a concrete reason to reject this pair, or is it only the alignment argument? I'd like your answer before the vote.

Leo, I don't see concrete evidence against your pair. Sam defending a team Sam is on is not, by itself, evidence of Evil. But a successful mission would not prove both of you are Good, since Evil can play Success, and a failure would not tell us which of you played Fail. I'd prefer a team including me because I know my own allegiance, but I recognize the rest of the table cannot verify that. I'm not treating the opening pairing or Omar's objections as proof of anyone's role.

Kenji’s point is fair: one mission result will not prove both Leo and I are Good, and I have not claimed it would. My point is narrower: Mission 1 is where the table can get its first real signal, and this two-person team is small enough that a failure cannot be diluted across a larger roster. Omar has now framed confidence as guilt repeatedly, but that is not concrete evidence; it is a reason to reject before seeing anything. If Amara has a specific objection to either Leo or me — not just the fact that we agree on the opening proposal — I want to hear it now, because that is the kind of information the table should act on. Otherwise, approving this team gives us a result and a public record, while rejecting it only changes the leader without resolving the same unknowns.

Sam asked directly whether I have a specific objection to either Leo or Sam, so I'll answer plainly: I don't. Neither of you has said or done anything that reads as evidence of Evil to me. Sam defending a team he's on is expected behavior, not a red flag, and Leo taking a seat on his own opening proposal is exactly the kind of accountability I want from a leader on Mission 1. Omar's alignment argument has some surface appeal, but I don't think it holds up under scrutiny. On the very first proposal, with no information available to anyone, every player who speaks is going to sound aligned with whoever they support — that's not a signal, it's just how a low-information game looks. Omar is right that rejection on Mission 1 costs us little structurally, but he's wrong that it costs us nothing: it costs us the first mission result, which is the only hard data this table can generate right now. A success tells us something useful, and a failure tells us the fault lies with Leo or Sam specifically, which is a very narrow and actionable result. Kenji made a fair point that a success doesn't clear either of them, since Evil can play Success, but the reverse is also true — a failure would be highly informative, and that's worth more than the alternative of shuffling leadership to another pair of unknowns. I'd also push back gently on Omar's framing that Leo and Sam are 'the most vocal and aligned.' Being vocal early is not a crime, and Omar himself has now spoken more than anyone at this table. If we treated repeated confident speech as suspicion, Omar would be the first under the microscope, and I don't think that's a standard any of us actually wants. My inclination is to approve this team. The leader has put his own name on it, the team is the minimum size so a failure is maximally diagnostic, and neither member has given me a concrete reason for doubt. If the vote goes the other way, I won't object to leadership rotating — but I'd rather we start generating information than start the game with rejections based on vibes. I'll be voting approve unless someone produces an actual reason to think Leo or Sam is compromised, not just a pattern they've constructed from the fact that two people agree with each other.

Amara and Kenji have now heard the same case: a two-person Mission 1 team gives the table the most diagnostic result, and no one has offered a concrete reason to think Sam or I is compromised. Omar keeps returning to the same alignment argument, and each time he has demanded rejection without naming a pair he would actually approve. That pattern matters more than the team itself. Kenji, you said you would prefer a team including you, but you also said the table cannot verify your allegiance. If this vote fails, which concrete pairing would you approve for Mission 1, and what would make you vote for this one instead?

Leo, if this proposal is rejected, I would support a team of Kenji and Leo: I know my own allegiance, and I have no concrete reason to suspect you. That preference is not evidence against Sam, and I recognize nobody else can verify my allegiance. I can also approve Leo and Sam as proposed; there is no solid public evidence against either of you. A failure would implicate at least one of you, while a success would not clear either of you.

Kenji's last answer is useful: he has no concrete evidence against Sam or me, and he says he can approve this pair as proposed. Omar has now made the same alignment argument several times without naming a pair he would approve, and the table should weigh that. A two-person Mission 1 team is the most diagnostic option we have. If it fails, the fault lies with one of two named players, and the table can adjust from there. I'm on the team and carry the same risk, so I'm not asking anyone to trust me on faith. I'm asking for a vote so the mission produces the first real signal. Omar, if you would approve a different pair, name it now and explain why it gives us more information than this team. Otherwise, the choice in front of the table is this team or a rejection that only rotates leadership without resolving any of the same unknowns.
Leo confirms Leo, Sam. Keeping Leo and Sam: a two-person Mission 1 team is the most diagnostic option, and rejecting it would only rotate leadership without resolving the same unknowns.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Amara, Kenji. Mission 1 succeeded, but my private information indicates Sam and Leo are Evil — they likely played Success to stay hidden. I will not include either on this team. Proposing myself, Amara, and Kenji: all three of us voted to approve Mission 1 and gave no indication of being compromised, and this team keeps Evil off a critical 3-player mission.

Omar’s proposal rests on a remarkable claim: that his private information indicates Leo and I are Evil. I know my own allegiance, and Mission 1 succeeded with Leo and me on it. That does not prove Leo is Good, but it directly contradicts the confidence of Omar’s claim. More importantly, in this ruleset private information is role-based, not a general investigative power. Omar, what exactly is the source of your private information, and why should the table accept an accusation you did not disclose before Mission 1’s vote? You spent Mission 1 demanding concrete evidence and warning against vibes; now you are asking us to approve a team built on an undisclosed private claim. That is a double standard. If your information is real, you should expect scrutiny of how you obtained it; if it is not, this proposal is an attempt to remove two players after a successful mission. I am not asking the table to approve me for Mission 2—I am asking them to notice that Omar’s rationale changed only after Mission 1 succeeded. His team also includes Amara and Kenji, both of whom approved Mission 1, so his “keep Evil off” framing is not supported by public behavior. I will vote based on whether Omar can substantiate this claim, not on his assertion alone.

Sam, you're asking me to publicly disclose the source of private role information — that is exactly what the rules say stays hidden. I am not going to do that, and the fact that you are demanding it tells me why you want it: you want to know what I know and who gave it to me. That is a question only someone with a reason to care about Merlin's knowledge would press this hard. My team selection is my prerogative as leader; I am entitled to weigh my judgment when choosing who sits on a critical three-player mission. You say my rationale changed after Mission 1 succeeded — it didn't. I had concerns about you and Leo during Mission 1's discussion, which is why I was the sole vote against the team. That pattern has been consistent from the first mission to this proposal. Mission 1 succeeding does not clear either of you, as Kenji correctly pointed out earlier: Evil players can and routinely do play Success on early missions to stay hidden. The structural reality is that Mission 1 succeeded, and whoever on that team played Fail would have been caught, so a clean pass is exactly what you would expect if at least one Evil player was on it and chose to hide. What matters now is what happens on Mission 2 with three seats. Amara, Kenji, and I all voted to approve Mission 1 with no red flags. I am proposing a team that excludes the two players my information points to. Amara, Kenji — Sam is asking me to reveal role-protected information to the table. Do you think that is a legitimate request, or is it telling that Sam is more interested in exposing my sources than in discussing whether the team is sound?

Omar asked Amara and Kenji directly whether Sam's demand for source disclosure is legitimate, so I'll answer since I'm on the proposed team. My answer is: no, not fully. In this game, the only private information that could name two specific Evil players is role-based sight, and asking someone to expose the source of that information is effectively asking them to paint a target on themselves or reveal their role to the Assassin. If Omar's information is real, pressing him to disclose it is exactly what an Evil player would want. So I won't vote against this team because Omar refused to burn his source.

That said, Omar's claim is still just his word, and I want to be precise about what the table actually knows. Mission 1 succeeded with Leo and Sam on it. That does not clear them — Kenji correctly noted early that Evil can play Success — but it means neither of them put down a Fail when one Fail would have failed the mission. Omar's story requires both of them to be Evil who chose to hide on a two-person mission where a single Fail card would have been caught. Possible, but it stacks assumptions.

Here is what actually makes me comfortable approving this team, and it is not trust in Omar's claim. Look at the structure of the roster. If Omar's information is genuine, this team contains no Evil and Mission 2 succeeds. If Omar is fabricating, then Omar himself is Evil, and this team fails regardless of who his partner is — whether the second Evil is Sam, Leo, or Kenji, the fail card comes from Omar or from a partner already on the roster. I know my own allegiance, so the outcome of this mission is essentially a direct referendum on Omar's credibility. If it succeeds, his claim gains real weight and the table should seriously reevaluate Leo and Sam. If it fails, Omar is exposed as the source of a false accusation, and I will treat him as the primary suspect for the rest of the game. Either result is hard information, which is more than rejecting the team and rotating leadership would give us.

One more thing, because it matters for how we read the room. Sam and Leo pushing back hard against Omar is expected behavior whether they are Good defending themselves or Evil protecting their position, so I'm not weighting it heavily in either direction. What I am weighting is that no one has produced a concrete contradiction of Omar's claim — only a challenge to its source, which I've already said is not a fair demand.

Omar, one direct question before the vote: if this mission fails, will you publicly accept that your own accusation makes you the prime suspect, and will you commit to that standard now rather than explaining it away afterward? I'd like your answer on the record, because it tells the table whether you're confident in your information or hedging.

Amara, yes — I'll answer your question on the record now. If Mission 2 fails, I accept that I become the prime suspect, because I'm the one who proposed this team and made the claim. That is exactly how it should work: I have staked my credibility on my information, and a failure means I either read it wrong or fabricated it. Either way, I will not explain it away — I will expect the table to scrutinize me first, and I'll accept that scrutiny.

I'm confident enough in my information to put that commitment in writing before the vote.

Now, to Sam's point: Sam asked why I didn't disclose my concerns before Mission 1's vote. I did — I was the sole vote against that team. My vote was my disclosure. What Sam is really objecting to is that I've now moved from quiet skepticism to acting on the information as leader. That is what a leader should do with private information: use it in team selection, not broadcast it.

Sam also says Mission 1's success 'directly contradicts' my claim. It doesn't. Evil players play Success routinely on early missions to stay hidden — Kenji and Amara both acknowledged this. On a two-player mission, one Fail card would have been caught immediately, so Evil had every reason to hide.

Amara laid out the logic precisely: if my information is real, this team is clean and Mission 2 succeeds. If I'm fabricating, then I'm Evil and this mission fails regardless. Either outcome is diagnostic. The mission result will speak for itself.

Amara's question and Omar's commitment are now on record. I accept the diagnostic standard: if this team fails, Omar is the prime suspect; if it succeeds, his claim gains weight, though it still does not prove Leo or me Evil, since Evil can play Success. I won't demand that Omar disclose role-protected information; Amara is right that doing so would only help Evil. My concern remains that Mission 1's success sits awkwardly with the confidence of Omar's accusation, but I recognize it does not disprove it. Given that this team excludes the Mission 1 pair and the result will be informative either way, I will vote to approve Omar, Amara, Kenji. If it fails, I expect Omar to keep the standard he just accepted.

I can support Omar, Amara, Kenji: I know my own allegiance, and this team tests a different group from Mission 1. But the proposed diagnostic is overstated. A failure would not by itself identify Omar rather than Amara, and a success would not prove Omar's claim, since Evil can play Success. Omar's private-information claim is worth considering, but the rest of us cannot verify it from his assertion alone. I intend to approve while keeping those limitations in mind.

Omar, I'm not comfortable approving this team, and I'll explain why. Your claim that Sam and I are Evil rests on private information you have refused to describe. You've committed to accepting suspicion if Mission 2 fails, which is a fair standard for your claim, but it doesn't give the table a reason to remove the two players from a team that just succeeded. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and me on it, and you were the only vote against that team. You called that vote a warning, and now it's the basis for an exclusion. Amara and Kenji have both said they can't verify your source. Kenji also pointed out that a success doesn't prove your claim and a failure doesn't identify you. So the table has an accusation, an exclusion, and no verification. I'm not asking anyone to trust me on faith. I'm asking the table to weigh whether one unverified claim should decide the roster. If your information is real, the table should ask what it's based on and whether it fits the Mission 1 result. I'd rather we reject this team and build a balanced proposal than approve a roster built on a claim nobody can check. Omar, you said you'd accept scrutiny if Mission 2 fails. Would you accept the same scrutiny if Mission 2 succeeds and your accusation against Sam and me turns out to be wrong?

Leo, yes — I accept scrutiny both ways. If Mission 2 succeeds and my information was wrong, I expect the table to treat me as having made a false accusation and to scrutinize me accordingly. I've staked my credibility on this claim in both directions.

But let's be clear about what your question is doing. You're asking me to accept suspicion if my claim is wrong while you yourself face no consequence for opposing a team that could be entirely clean. If this mission succeeds with three players I trust on it, your objection will look exactly like what I believe it is: a defense of a roster you want back on future teams.

You say the table should ask what my information is based on. I understand the instinct, but role-based information stays hidden by design — that's what protects the source. What I can tell you is this: I was consistent from the first moment of this game. I was the sole vote against Leo and Sam before any mission result existed, and I've maintained that position through Mission 1's success. That consistency is public and verifiable.

Leo, you asked whether I'd accept scrutiny if my accusation turns out wrong. I've answered yes on the record. Here's my question back to you: if Mission 2 succeeds with this team, will you accept that your persistent opposition to excluding you and Sam — from the very first mission through now — is the pattern that deserves scrutiny next?

Omar, I'm voting against this team, and my reason is the same as before. Your accusation against Sam and me rests on private information you will not describe, and now you are asking the table to exclude both of us from a team right after Mission 1 succeeded. Mission 1's result does not clear anyone, and you already agreed that Evil can play Success. So the table has an accusation, an exclusion, and no way to verify either one. Amara's roster logic only works if we trust the claim, and Kenji has already said the table cannot verify it. Omar, you say your vote against Sam and me was your disclosure, but the table learned nothing from it except suspicion. A leader who excludes two players on an unverifiable basis is asking everyone to gamble a mission on his word. Kenji, you said you can approve while keeping those limits in mind. Given that the claim cannot be checked, would you prefer a balanced proposal that includes one of the Mission 1 players over a roster that depends on Omar's assertion?

Leo, I don't prefer adding a Mission 1 player simply for balance. Its success doesn't clear either of you, and including me gives me confidence in one seat. Omar's claim remains unverified, but this roster doesn't require accepting it as fact. I still intend to approve, and I'll interpret either result cautiously: a failure wouldn't identify the culprit, and a success wouldn't prove the team clean.

Omar, for the record: I'm voting against Omar, Amara, Kenji. Nothing in this discussion has verified the claim that Sam and I are Evil, and Omar still hasn't said what it rests on. Amara's roster logic only works if that claim is true, and Kenji has said the table cannot verify it. Omar has also agreed to accept scrutiny only after the mission result, so the team itself is the only thing being tested. Rejecting this roster costs us a leader change. Approving it means sending three players on a mission based on one unchecked accusation. I'd rather we build a proposal the table can check against the public record before anyone is excluded on private information.

Leo, the question you asked Omar — whether he would accept scrutiny if Mission 2 succeeds and his accusation is wrong — has already been answered on the record: yes, both ways. He committed to that before the vote, and he restated it when you asked again. So that objection is spent. What remains of your case is that his claim is unverifiable, and I agree with that — Kenji agrees with that, Omar himself has not disputed it. But here is the problem: every roster decision available to this table on Mission 2 rests on unverifiable claims. You cannot verify my allegiance. Kenji cannot prove his. If you become leader, you will select a team based on nothing but your own unprovable assertion that you and Sam are clean — which is exactly the same epistemic situation, just with the accusation removed because it names you. You have now made your case multiple times and have not once offered a concrete alternative roster you would actually approve. Rejecting this team does not produce a proposal 'the table can check against the public record'; no such proposal exists at this stage of the game. It produces a leadership rotation and a fresh set of unverifiable claims. Meanwhile, the structure of this roster remains genuinely diagnostic. I know my own seat. If Mission 2 fails, the fault lies with Omar or Kenji — and given Omar's stated information, a failure also exposes his accusation as false, which is exactly the standard he accepted. A success gives his claim real weight against Leo and Sam. Either outcome is hard data, which rejection cannot provide. Sam and Kenji have both said they intend to approve. My vote is approve, and I encourage the table to generate the result rather than rotate leadership into the same fog.

I still intend to approve Omar, Amara, Kenji. But I disagree with Amara's certainty about the result: a failure would implicate Omar or Amara from my perspective, not establish which one is Evil or prove Omar fabricated his claim. A success would be useful, but Evil can play Success, so it would not verify his accusation against Leo and Sam. We should keep those possibilities open when interpreting the result.

Amara’s last statement changes my view. I cannot approve Omar, Amara, Kenji on the basis she offered. A clean result on this roster cannot verify Omar’s claim about Leo and me, because neither of us is on the team; Evil can play Success, and a success would only show that no one on Omar, Amara, Kenji played Fail. It would not make Omar’s accusation against Leo and me more checkable or stronger. Omar has converted an unverified private claim into a roster exclusion and a later scrutiny promise. That is a credibility wager, not public evidence. I accept that if this team fails, Omar is the prime suspect, but I do not accept that if it succeeds the table should treat his accusation as confirmed. The public record still contains only Omar’s assertion, my denial, and a Mission 1 success. I will vote against this team because its stated diagnostic value is overstated and it excludes two players on an accusation the table cannot test.

Sam, I want to address your reversal directly, because it matters. In your earlier statement you accepted the diagnostic standard, acknowledged that Omar had committed to scrutiny in both directions, and said — in your own words — that you would vote to approve Omar, Amara, Kenji. Now, after Kenji simply cautioned against overstating what the result would prove, you have flipped to reject. Kenji's caution is correct and I never disputed it: a success does not verify Omar's claim, and a failure does not by itself identify a culprit. But that caution existed before you announced your approval, and it does not justify abandoning it. What changed between your two statements is that I explained why I find this roster worthwhile despite the unverifiability of Omar's claim. If my explanation is what moved you from approve to reject, the table should notice that my reasoning gave you nothing new — only the observation that every possible Mission 2 roster rests on unverifiable claims, which is simply true of any five-player game at this stage.

So let me restate my position precisely, adopting Kenji's corrections rather than the certainty you attribute to me. If this mission fails, the fault lies with someone on the roster, and Omar's accusation is exposed as unreliable — by his own on-record commitment, he becomes the prime suspect. That part of the diagnostic stands regardless of whether we can pinpoint the Fail card. If this mission succeeds, we learn only that no one on this team played Fail. That is still real information: it eliminates three seats from suspicion for this mission and gives Omar's claim weight as a hypothesis, not proof. Sam, you say the diagnostic value is overstated — I have already conceded the part that was overstated. What you have not explained is why the correct response to a partially diagnostic roster is a rejection that produces no result at all.

The vote arithmetic is now visible: Leo and Sam against, Omar and Kenji for, and me. I confirm I am voting to approve. Leo has also declined, across multiple turns, to name any roster he would actually approve, and Sam's reversal came only after it became clear his earlier approval was on record. I leave it to the table to weigh why the two players accused by Omar's claim are also the two most motivated to prevent this mission from generating a result. I am not treating that motivation as proof of anything — but I am noting that a rejection here serves exactly the players the accusation names, and no one else. Send this team and let the mission speak.

Omar confirms Omar, Amara, Kenji. I'm confident in this roster: Omar, Amara, and Kenji have all been consistent, voted responsibly, and none are implicated by anything in the public record. Mission 2 succeeds or fails informatively with these three, and I'm not revising a lineup I trust.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Amara proposes Amara, Omar. I am a Loyal Servant, so I know my own seat is Good. Omar's claim against Leo and Sam gained real weight when Mission 2 succeeded — he committed on the record to scrutiny in both directions, and the result came back clean with him on the roster. Leo and Sam, meanwhile, both voted against a clean roster and worked to prevent Mission 2 from generating any result. Pairing myself with Omar gives the table one verified-Good seat and one player whose credibility has been publicly tested and upheld. A success here moves us to 3-0; a failure would sharply implicate Omar's claim and expose him.

Mission 2 succeeded, but that does not verify Omar’s accusation or clear anyone on the team: Evil can play Success. Likewise, Amara’s claim to be a Loyal Servant is not verifiable by the rest of us.

For a mission that could secure our third success, I would prefer Amara and Kenji because I know my own allegiance and have no conclusive reason to distrust Amara. I recognize that the rest of the table cannot verify my allegiance either. I’ll consider the proposed Amara, Omar team, but we should not treat either previous success as proof that its members are Good.

I will vote to approve Amara, Omar. I still do not treat Omar’s earlier claim as proven, and I disagree with the way it was used to exclude Leo and me from Mission 2. But Mission 2 came back clean with Omar on the roster, and Amara has now proposed the minimum team size at a point where the table needs a result rather than another leadership rotation. A failure here would fall directly on Amara or Omar and would sharply damage Omar’s credibility; a success would move us to three successes and force the next phase of the game. I am not saying either outcome proves anyone’s allegiance, since Evil can play Success. I am saying this roster is small, testable, and better than spending another proposal cycle on the same unresolved accusations. My vote is approve.

Sam, a small team is useful, but this mission could end the mission phase, so a failure is more than a test. Mission 2’s success does not clear Omar or Amara. I still prefer Amara and Kenji because I know my own allegiance, though I understand the rest of you cannot verify it. I’m not treating Omar’s claim as proven or accusing either member of the proposed team.

I'm going to support Amara and Omar. Mission 2 came back clean with Omar on the roster, and a two-person team is the smallest test we can run for Mission 3. I still don't think the table should treat Omar's claim as settled, and I haven't retracted my concerns about how it was used to exclude Sam and me from Mission 2. But another proposal cycle spent on the same unverifiable accusations doesn't help anyone. Amara has said she is a Loyal Servant, and I'll take her at her word for now while the mission shows us more. The record is clear that Good has already won two missions, so this is the moment to generate a result rather than rotate leadership again. My vote is approve.

Kenji raised two fair cautions, and I want to address both directly. First, he is right that neither of our previous successes proves anyone Good — I have never claimed otherwise, and I will not claim it now. Second, he is right that my claim to be a Loyal Servant is not verifiable by the table. I accept both points as stated.

But here is what the table should weigh when comparing his preferred roster of Amara and Kenji against my proposed Amara and Omar. I know my own seat is Good. That is the one piece of private knowledge I can put to structural use as leader, and I am using it to make Mission 3 maximally diagnostic. If this team fails, the Fail card came from Omar — not from me, and not shared with a third unknown. That is the sharpest possible test of the single most important open question at this table: whether Omar's accusation against Leo and Sam was genuine or fabricated. A failure with me on the roster does not merely implicate 'someone on the team'; combined with my stated role, it isolates Omar exactly, and by his own on-record commitments he has already accepted that standard. If it succeeds, we move to 3-0 and the table can carry Omar's claim forward with real weight behind it.

Compare that to Amara and Kenji: a failure there would implicate me or Kenji from the table's perspective, which muddies rather than clarifies, and it would leave Omar's accusation untested for another round. Kenji's preference is understandable — everyone prefers a seat they can vouch for — but swapping Omar out does not produce better information; it produces vaguer information on the question that actually matters.

To Kenji's caution that a success here would not end the game or verify everything: agreed, and I am not asking the table to treat it as proof. I am asking for the most informative two-seat roster available, and I believe this is it. Sam has approved, Leo has approved despite his earlier objections, and the swing consideration is Kenji's. Kenji, I will ask you directly: given that you have stated you have no conclusive reason to distrust me, that you are not accusing either member of this team, and that a failure on Amara and Omar pinpoints Omar precisely while a success secures the third mission — is there a concrete reason left for you to reject this roster, or will you approve it? If you have one, name it now before the vote; if not, I would welcome your approval on the record.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
